strengths: The paper identifies a novel and economically relevant vulnerability in the dominant pay-per-token pricing model: because tokenization of a fixed output string is not unique and users cannot observe the true generative token sequence, providers have an incentive to misreport tokenizations and overcharge.

It formalizes the interaction as a principal-agent problem and provides a clean taxonomy of provider incentives, including the observation that under pay-per-token the provider wants the longest valid tokenization and that reporting each character as a separate token can inflate bills by roughly 3x in the authors' experiments.

The theoretical results are interesting and nontrivial: Theorem 3 and its extensions establish NP-hardness of finding the longest plausible tokenization under top-p/top-k sampling or a probability threshold, via a reduction from Hamiltonian path.

Theorem 6 gives a useful characterization of additive incentive-compatible pricing mechanisms: any such mechanism must price linearly in character counts, and equal per-character pricing yields a unique pay-per-character scheme. This is a simple but strong design insight.

The empirical section provides a proof-of-concept for the practical threat: Algorithm 1 finds plausible longer tokenizations and can overcharge by up to ~13% in some settings, with confidence intervals, multiple open models, and additional results in the appendix.

The limitations and broader-impact discussion is candid, acknowledging dual-use risk, model assumptions, and that the proposed pricing change would likely require external regulation or user pressure.
weaknesses: The formal definition of incentive-compatibility (Definition 4) omits the critical restriction that the reported token sequence must represent the same output string. As written, it would imply all token sequences have equal reward, contradicting Theorem 6; the proof of Proposition 5 implicitly relies on a same-string constraint that is not stated. This is a central formal flaw that should be corrected.

The NP-hardness reduction includes the end-of-sequence token ∅ in the vocabulary and in the plausibility sets. If ∅ can be appended without changing the string, the reduction's decision criterion can be trivially satisfied, weakening the proof. The treatment of special tokens needs clarification.

The claim that pay-per-character 'completely eliminates' the financial incentive is overstated. It removes the incentive to misreport tokenization of a fixed string, but providers could still manipulate the output string (e.g., adding invisible characters), misreport next-token distributions, or exploit other undisclosed parts of the generative process. The authors note some of these as future work, so the central claim should be scoped more carefully.

The empirical evaluation is limited: it focuses on temperatures above 1.15, high top-p values, 400 LMSYS prompts, 200-300 token outputs, and open-weight models. The heuristic overcharge is modest (0.3%-13%) and sometimes zero (e.g., Gemma-3-4B at lower temperatures), so the practical severity is not fully established.

Algorithm 1's core choice--splitting the highest-vocabulary-index token--lacks theoretical justification and may be tokenizer-specific. There is no guarantee that it finds a longer plausible tokenization, and the optimal number of iterations is chosen empirically without a principled stopping rule.

Reproducibility is only moderate: the paper provides hardware, datasets, model names, and generation settings, but does not release code, and there are minor appendix typos (e.g., listing Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct twice where 1B/3B are likely intended).

The paper does not deeply discuss practical deployment obstacles for transparency or pay-per-character pricing, such as proprietary tokenizers, international Unicode/character-count ambiguities, and whether users or regulators can realistically enforce the proposed contract.

strengths: The paper studies a timely and practically relevant question: how pay-per-token pricing in LLM-as-a-service creates incentives for providers to misreport token counts.
It gives a clear principal-agent formalization of delegated autoregressive generation and tokenization misreporting.

The NP-hardness result for finding the longest plausible tokenization under top-p/top-k sampling (Theorem 3) is a nice theoretical contribution and is supported by a plausible reduction from Hamiltonian path.
The heuristic Algorithm 1, while simple, provides a proof-of-concept showing that transparency about next-token distributions does not automatically eliminate overcharging.
The proposed pay-per-character pricing mechanism and the characterization of additive incentive-compatible mechanisms are useful starting points for discussion.
The limitations and broader-impact sections acknowledge some practical and ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Definition 4 is formally flawed: it omits the restriction that the reported token sequence must preserve the generated string. As written, no nonconstant pricing mechanism can satisfy it, because a provider can always report a longer, different string and receive higher reward. The proof of Proposition 5 would then force r to be constant, contradicting Theorem 6. The central incentive-compatibility result is therefore not sound as stated.

The paper overclaims its contribution: the abstract/introduction imply that pay-per-character completely eliminates the financial incentive to strategize and that any incentive-compatible mechanism must price tokens linearly on character count. The latter is false unless one restricts to additive mechanisms; under same-string reporting, any function of the output string is incentive-compatible. The former ignores new moral hazards under pay-per-character, such as padding outputs with zero-width or invisible characters or generating verbose outputs to inflate the character count without increasing user value.

The proposed pay-per-character mechanism has unaddressed strategic loopholes. Providers could append invisible Unicode characters or otherwise manipulate the reported string to increase billed characters while preserving perceived content, so the mechanism does not fully eliminate overcharging incentives.

The experimental setting is not representative of the motivating threat. All experiments use open-weight models with public tokenizers, whereas the vulnerability is most relevant for proprietary providers whose tokenizers and internal distributions are not observable. No actual user-provider misreporting simulation or API audit is performed.

The headline empirical claim is heavily conditional. The reported maximum overcharge of ~13% occurs only for p=0.99 and temperature 1.3; at p=0.95 and p=0.90 the overcharge drops to ~2.6% and ~0.3%. Such high temperature and permissive top-p settings limit practical impact. There is also an inconsistency: Table 1 reports over 300% overcharge while the text describes this as ~3x, which is numerically inconsistent.

Algorithm 1 is underspecified and its pseudocode is inconsistent (mixing t and ¯t). It does not explain what happens when no valid token pair can split a token, and the stated O(m(log m + σ_max)) complexity is not justified. No code, random seeds, or exact prompt lists are provided, limiting reproducibility.

The paper does not convincingly show that NP-hardness matters in practice; the same paper demonstrates a simple heuristic that succeeds, so the 'hard to misreport without suspicion' narrative is weakened. The empirical evaluation also lacks stronger statistical rigor (large confidence intervals, no significance tests).

The pay-per-character mechanism may misalign provider cost and reward across languages, scripts, and content types, potentially creating cross-subsidies or discouraging certain outputs. The paper does not analyze these downstream effects.

strengths: Novel and timely problem: identifies an economic vulnerability in pay-per-token LLM APIs due to non-unique tokenization, and frames it as a principal-agent problem.

Solid theoretical framing: formalizes provider incentives, proves NP-hardness of finding longest plausible tokenization under top-p/top-k/threshold, and characterizes additive incentive-compatible pricing as linear in character counts (once properly restricted).

Practical proof-of-concept: introduces a simple heuristic that empirically finds plausible longer tokenizations, demonstrating up to ~13% overcharge under transparency across several open LLMs and LMSYS prompts.
Actionable proposal: pay-per-character pricing is simple, has a clear transition path (r_c = r0/cpt), and creates positive incentives for more efficient tokenization.
Reproducibility and honesty: experimental setup, models, dataset, hardware, seeds, and confidence intervals are documented; limitations, broader impact, and ethical concerns are discussed.
weaknesses: Major formal flaw in the incentive-compatibility definition: Definition 4 allows any reported sequence, including a different string with more characters. Under this definition, pay-per-character is not incentive-compatible (a provider can report a longer string for higher reward), and the proof of Proposition 5 would imply all rewards are constant. Theorem 6 is therefore false as stated. The definition and proof must explicitly restrict reports to str(hat t)=str(t).

Hardness proof gap: the reduction permits appending the end-of-sequence token ∅ to a^λ, yielding a plausible length-2 sequence regardless of Hamiltonian path. The theorem needs to exclude EOS from reported sequences or handle it explicitly; similar care is needed in the extensions.

Overclaiming: the abstract/intro state that any incentive-compatible mechanism must price linearly on character count, but Theorem 6 only covers additive mechanisms. The additive restriction should be stated wherever the result is summarized.

Empirical scope and impact: the heuristic overcharge is shown only at temperatures >1.0 (1.15, 1.30, 1.45) and with top-p; standard temperature 1.0 or lower is not demonstrated. The subtle overcharge (~13%) is modest, and the trivial ~3x overcharge may be easily detected, so the practical severity is not fully established.

Reproducibility and presentation: no code/artifact release is mentioned; some details are inconsistent (e.g., 90% CI t-value with 5 repetitions, duplicate model names, 'Gemma-3-1B-In' in Table 1, Eq. 4 says t∈V instead of V*). Algorithm 1's claimed complexity is not fully justified.
The mechanism design result, as currently formalized, does not support the paper's central proposed solution; revisions are needed before others can reliably build on the pay-per-character claim.

strengths: The paper identifies a novel and timely economic vulnerability in LLM-as-a-service: because tokenization is not unique, pay-per-token pricing gives providers an incentive to misreport the tokenization of an output while preserving its text.

It formalizes the interaction as a principal-agent problem and provides a clean theoretical characterization of incentive-compatible additive pricing: under string-preserving reporting, any additive incentive-compatible mechanism must price linearly in character counts, yielding pay-per-character as essentially the unique such mechanism among additive schemes.

The NP-hardness results for finding the longest plausible tokenization under top-p sampling, top-k sampling, and probability-threshold plausibility are technically interesting and complement the practical heuristic.

The empirical study is reasonably broad across Llama, Gemma, and Ministral families, uses LMSYS prompts, and measures both overcharging and financial profitability, including GPU energy measurements for generation versus verification.

The pay-per-character proposal is accompanied by a simple transition prescription (r_c = r_o * tpc) that maintains average profit margin, and the paper analyzes how margins vary across tokens and languages, showing a language-fairness side benefit.

Reproducibility appears adequate: model versions, hardware, dataset filtering, sampling settings, confidence intervals, and energy-measurement methodology are reported. The limitations section is unusually honest about model assumptions, enforcement gaps, and broader impact.
weaknesses: Definition 4 of incentive-compatibility is formally under-specified/too broad. As written, it quantifies over arbitrary reporting policies, so a provider could report a different, longer string and profit even under pay-per-character. The intended restriction to string-preserving tokenization misreporting should be explicit. The abstract also overclaims that any incentive-compatible mechanism must be character-linear, whereas Theorem 6 is specifically about additive mechanisms.

The transparency-based hardness argument assumes that providers truthfully report next-token distributions or probabilities. If providers can lie about those distributions, the user cannot verify plausibility, and the main mitigation collapses. The paper acknowledges this indirectly in limitations but does not resolve it, leaving a gap between the theoretical threat model and deployable practice.

The demonstrated overcharging is modest for realistic sampling settings: for p=0.95 and p=0.90 the reported gains are only about 1.8% and 0.28%, respectively, and experiments use a high temperature of 1.3. This limits the practical severity of the vulnerability under common API configurations.

The energy-cost assumption that verification cost c_v is constant and independent of token-sequence length is questionable. A forward pass to score a tokenization should scale with sequence length, even if the measured verification cost is small relative to generation cost. The profitability condition may be sensitive to this approximation.

The analysis is restricted to open-weight models and does not test proprietary APIs, hidden reasoning tokens, or model-substitution attacks. Pay-per-character also does not eliminate other moral hazards such as verbosity inflation, model substitution, or misreporting internal reasoning tokens; some are acknowledged but they reduce the scope of the proposed fix.

There are minor presentation/notation inconsistencies (e.g., t, tilde-t, and hat-t are used with shifting meanings), and no code/artifact link is mentioned, which slightly weakens reproducibility despite otherwise detailed experimental reporting.

strengths: The core observation is novel and timely: because a string admits many tokenizations, a pay-per-token provider can inflate the reported token count without changing the text the user receives, and the framing of this as a principal-agent/moral-hazard problem is apt and clearly motivated.

Theorem 6 (with Proposition 5) is a clean and genuinely useful characterization: within the additive family, incentive compatibility holds if and only if the price is linear in per-character counts. This is the strongest and most non-obvious theoretical contribution.

Theorem 3 establishes NP-hardness of finding the longest top-p-plausible tokenization via a Hamiltonian-path reduction, and the appendices extend it to top-k sampling and to a sequence-probability-threshold criterion, giving a coherent story for why transparency constrains optimal misreporting.

The empirical study spans several model families and tokenizers (Llama, Gemma, Ministral), and Section 3.3 / Eq. 4 / Table 1 attempt to close the loop by comparing the additional revenue from misreporting against the GPU energy cost of the plausibility check, which is the right kind of analysis for a profitability claim.
The limitations discussion is honest and fairly thorough (verbosity inflation under pay-per-character, micro-level scope, LMSYS prompt non-representativeness, inability to test proprietary models).
weaknesses: Central claim is overstated. The abstract/intro state that 'any incentive-compatible pricing mechanism must price tokens linearly on their character count,' but Theorem 6 only establishes this for additive mechanisms. Non-additive incentive-compatible mechanisms (e.g., any mechanism whose price depends only on the string, such as a nonlinear function of |str(t)|) are not characterized and are not excluded, so the sweeping claim is not supported by the theorem as written.

The headline 'significantly overcharge users' is not well supported by the evidence. Under realistic sampling the effect is tiny: ~1.8% (p=0.95) and ~0.28% (p=0.90). The large overcharges (up to ~11% for p=0.99, and the ~300% in Fig. 1a) require either near-full-distribution sampling or Algorithm 1, which produces implausible tokenizations that are trivially detectable—precisely the case the paper argues is uninteresting. The dramatic framing in the title/abstract is not matched by the demonstrated magnitude.

The threat/defense model is muddled and partly circular. The paper assumes the provider is 'obliged to be transparent' about next-token distributions, but an adversarial provider can also misreport those distributions or use a different internal tokenizer (the authors acknowledge this), so the user cannot independently verify 'plausibility' without TEEs/ZK proofs—which are deferred to future work. As a result, the user's ability to 'contest' a tokenization is not grounded, weakening the practical force of both the attack and the transparency-based mitigation.

The proposed fix is under-delivered. Once Proposition 5 is in hand, 'price the string' is nearly immediate, and the paper itself concedes pay-per-character does not prevent verbosity inflation, so the abstract's claim that it 'eliminate[s] the financial incentive to strategize' overstates what is actually achieved (it removes only the tokenization-misreporting incentive).

Questionable/inadequately justified modeling assumption. The claim that the verification cost c_v is independent of the sequence and its length (Section 3.3, Table 1) conflicts with the usual O(L^2) prefill/attention scaling and is reported as a single constant per model; this needs stronger justification, and it is load-bearing for the Eq. 4 profitability condition. There is also a hardware inconsistency (Appendix A says 2xA100, while Fig. 11/Table 1 say a single H100), which is a reproducibility concern.

Narrow empirical scope. All experiments use small open-weight models (1B–8B); the actual commercial providers are frontier proprietary models that are not tested. Algorithm 2 is a heuristic with no guarantees, and its design choices (split the highest-index token into the pair with maximum minimum index) are unmotivated and not compared against alternatives or ablated.

The incentive analysis ignores detection/reputation and detection probability: for a provider, a 1–11% revenue bump must be weighed against the risk of being caught, and the paper does not model this. Without it, the claim that misreporting is 'financially worthwhile' in practice is incomplete.

strengths: Timely and novel framing: the paper is (to my knowledge) the first to analyze the economic incentives created by the ubiquitous pay-per-token pricing of LLM-as-a-service, casting tokenization (mis-)reporting as a principal–agent problem with information asymmetry and moral hazard.

Clean and general theoretical characterization (Theorem 6, Corollary 7): an additive pricing mechanism is incentive-compatible if and only if it prices tokens linearly on their character counts, so the unique equal-price IC mechanism is pay-per-character. The proof via Proposition 5 and the single-character tokenization is elegant and correct, and the corollary that pay-per-token is provably not incentive-compatible is a crisp, quotable result.

The NP-hardness of finding the longest top-p-plausible tokenization (Theorem 3), with extensions to top-k sampling and a probability-threshold plausibility criterion, is a well-constructed reduction from Hamiltonian path and complements the practical heuristic nicely.

Algorithm 2 is a simple, transparent, and reproducible heuristic that demonstrably finds plausible longer tokenizations, with empirical validation across Llama, Gemma, and Ministral families and LMSYS prompts. The financial-viability analysis (Eq. 4) is a useful bridge from overcharging percentages to provider utility and profit margins.

Reproducibility is good: public models and datasets, described hardware, measured energy costs (Table 1, Figure 11), and clear experimental protocol with confidence intervals. The limitations and broader-impact sections are unusually thorough and honest (including the dual-use risk of the heuristic).
weaknesses: Definition 4 of incentive-compatibility is stated over *any* reporting policy, but the analysis (and the converse direction of Theorem 6) implicitly restricts to string-preserving policies. Under the literal definition, no output-length-based mechanism—including pay-per-character—is IC, since a provider could report a longer (different) string for more revenue. The definition should be restricted to policies that preserve str(t); this gap affects the formal validity of the claimed characterization and should be fixed.

The evaluation is confined to open-weight models (Llama, Gemma, Ministral). The vulnerability is arguably most consequential for proprietary providers whose tokenizers/next-token distributions users cannot inspect, yet this setting is not (and perhaps cannot easily be) tested.

The profitability argument hinges on the claim that the per-output verification cost c_v is constant and independent of sequence length. This is surprising—a longer token sequence should cost more to verify—and is supported only over the narrow 200–300-token range in Figure 11. Since the provider's modified sequence is longer (more tokens), the relevant c_v may not equal the measured one; this deserves more careful justification, as Eq. 4 depends on it.

The practical severity is limited: overcharging is only substantial at high top-p (11.2% at p=0.99) and collapses to 1.8% (p=0.95) and 0.28% (p=0.90), and requires high temperature (1.3). Under settings commonly used in production, the demonstrated gain is modest, which tempers the headline 'overcharging' claim.

The hardness result is essentially a negative result that the paper's own heuristic circumvents in practice; its practical bite is therefore limited, as the authors acknowledge. It reads more as context than as a binding constraint on provider behavior.

Pay-per-character is not a complete remedy: it does not prevent verbosity inflation, and it produces variable (sometimes negative) margins, notably for underrepresented languages (Figure 12). The 'maintain average margin' prescription is reasonable but leaves these distributional issues only partially addressed.
